steps.heading: Why start here?
steps.body: Every model of consumer choice in this module has the same two-part structure: what the consumer WANTS (preferences, covered next lesson) and what they CAN AFFORD (the budget constraint, covered here). You can't say anything about a person's choice without first pinning down their feasible set — the menu of bundles they could possibly buy. That's what this lesson builds.

steps.heading: Setting it up
steps.body:
Take the simplest case: two goods, good 1 (quantity x1, price P1) and good 2 (quantity x2, price P2), and income M. If the consumer spends everything, total spending equals income:

P1x1 + P2x2 = M

This is the budget constraint. Every symbol here is exogenous (given from outside the model, not explained by it) except x1 and x2, which are endogenous — the things we're trying to predict.

steps.q: In the budget constraint P1x1 + P2x2 = M, which variable is endogenous?
options: P1, the price of good 1
M, income
x1 and x2, the quantities chosen
All four are exogenous
steps.explain: P1, P2 and M are all taken as given (exogenous) — they're set by the market or the consumer's circumstances, not explained by the model. x1 and x2, the quantities the consumer chooses, are what the model is trying to determine (endogenous).

steps.heading: Drawing it: rearrange for the graph
steps.body:
To plot this with x2 on the vertical axis and x1 on the horizontal axis, solve for x2:

x2 = M/P2 - (P1/P2)x1

This is just a straight line: y = intercept - (slope)·x, with 'y' being x2 and 'x' being x1. The vertical intercept, M/P2, is what you'd get if you spent your entire income on good 2 alone. The horizontal intercept (where x2=0), M/P1, is spending it all on good 1.

steps.q: A consumer has M=£200, P1=£10 (good 1, on the horizontal axis), P2=£5 (good 2, vertical axis). What is the horizontal intercept?
options: 20 units
40 units
5 units
steps.explain: Horizontal intercept = M/P1 = 200/10 = 20 units. If you got 40, you divided by the wrong price — that's M/P2 = 200/5 = 40, which is the VERTICAL intercept (all income spent on good 2) instead.

steps.heading: The slope is the real economics
steps.body: The slope of the budget line is -P1/P2. This isn't just a graphing detail — it's the rate at which the MARKET lets you trade good 1 for good 2. You can derive it directly: hold spending fixed at M, and ask how much x2 must change if x1 changes by a small amount Δx1. Differencing the constraint gives P1Δx1 + P2Δx2 = 0, so Δx2/Δx1 = -P1/P2. This ratio is called the marginal rate of transformation (MRT) — how many units of good 2 the MARKET requires you to give up for one more unit of good 1. It's purely a function of prices; it has nothing to do with how much the consumer personally likes either good — that's a separate question for the next lesson.

steps.q: Why is the price of good 1 (the good on the horizontal axis) on TOP of the slope formula -P1/P2, rather than P2 on top?
options: It's an arbitrary labelling convention with no deeper meaning
Because good 1's price determines how many units of good 2 you sacrifice per extra unit of good 1 — the sacrificed good's price sits on the bottom, the gained good's price on top
Because P1 is always larger than P2 in practice
Because the vertical axis good's price must always be in the denominator regardless of context
steps.explain: It falls straight out of the algebra: Δx2/Δx1 = -P1/P2 comes from P1Δx1 = -P2Δx2. Economically: buying one more unit of good 1 costs P1; to free up that much money you must give up P1/P2 units of good 2 (since each unit of good 2 is worth P2). The good you're buying more of has its price on top.

steps.heading: What moves the line: income vs prices
steps.body:
Two very different kinds of shift, and exam questions love testing whether you can tell them apart:

- A change in income M, with both prices fixed, shifts the line PARALLEL to itself (same slope -P1/P2, both intercepts scale by the same amount). More income → outward parallel shift; less → inward.
- A change in a SINGLE price rotates the line around the OTHER good's intercept. If P1 rises, the horizontal intercept M/P1 shrinks (you can afford less of good 1), but the vertical intercept M/P2 is untouched (P2 and M haven't changed) — so the line pivots inward around that fixed vertical point, becoming steeper.
- If BOTH prices change by the same proportion (e.g. both double) with income fixed, that's mathematically identical to income falling by that proportion with prices fixed — a parallel inward shift, because the ratio P1/P2 (the slope) is unchanged.

steps.q: PX rises while PY and M stay fixed. What happens to the budget line?
options: Parallel outward shift
Parallel inward shift
Pivots inward around the Y-intercept, becoming steeper (in absolute slope)
Pivots inward around the X-intercept, becoming flatter
steps.explain: The Y-intercept (M/PY) is untouched since PY and M are unchanged. The X-intercept (M/PX) shrinks since PX rose. The line pivots around the fixed Y-intercept, and since X is now relatively more expensive, the line becomes steeper (the consumer sacrifices more Y per unit of X).

steps.heading: One subtlety: kinked budget constraints
steps.body: Not every budget line is a single straight segment. If a good has a bulk discount (price drops after some threshold quantity), or a wage rate changes after a certain number of hours worked (think overtime pay, or a labour-leisure choice where the wage rises after 40 hours), the budget 'line' bends at that threshold — it's piecewise linear with a kink. The general principle is unchanged: work out the slope (relative price / trade-off rate) on EACH segment separately, and the kink sits exactly at the quantity where the price regime changes. You'll meet these again when optimising — a kink can itself become the optimal choice, which the standard tangency condition can't handle directly (covered in the Constrained Optimisation lesson).

steps.heading: From 'can afford' to 'wants'
steps.body: The budget constraint told us what's feasible. Now we need a way to describe what the consumer WANTS, so we can predict which feasible bundle they'll actually pick. Economists do this with a preference ordering: given any two bundles X=(x1,x2) and Y=(y1,y2), the consumer can say X≻Y (strictly prefers X), Y≻X, or X∽Y (indifferent).

steps.heading: The three basic axioms
steps.body:
For this ordering to be usable at all, we assume three things hold:

1. Completeness — any two bundles CAN be compared; there's no pair where the consumer simply has no opinion.
2. Transitivity — if X≽Y and Y≽Z, then X≽Z. Without this, you could get preference cycles (X≻Y≻Z≻X) where there's no well-defined 'best' bundle at all.
3. Continuity — if X is preferred to Y, then bundles very close to Y are still less preferred than X (no sudden jumps). This is what allows us to draw preferences as smooth curves rather than a scatter of disconnected points.

steps.q: A consumer's stated preferences are: Apple≻Banana, Banana≻Cherry, and Cherry≻Apple. Which axiom is violated?
options: Completeness
Transitivity
Continuity
None — this is a perfectly valid preference ordering
steps.explain: This is a textbook transitivity violation — the three preferences form a cycle with no top element. If asked 'what's the best of these three?', there's no consistent answer.

steps.heading: Well-behaved preferences: monotonicity and convexity
steps.body:
Two extra assumptions make preferences 'well-behaved' and give us the familiar downward-sloping, bowed-in indifference curves you'll have seen in every textbook diagram:

- Monotonicity (more is better): if bundle Y has at least as much of both goods as X, and strictly more of at least one, then Y≻X. This rules out 'bads' and satiation, and it's why indifference curves must slope downward — if you take some of good 1 away, you MUST be given some of good 2 back to stay equally happy.
- Convexity: averages are (weakly) preferred to extremes. If you're indifferent between X and Y, any weighted mix z=(tx1+(1-t)y1, tx2+(1-t)y2) for 0<t<1 is at least as good as either. This is what makes indifference curves bow toward the origin rather than bow outward or zig-zag.

steps.q: A consumer's indifference curves are straight lines with a constant slope everywhere. Are their preferences still convex?
options: No — convexity requires curves to bow strictly inward, and a straight line doesn't bow at all
Yes — a straight line satisfies convexity weakly (as an equality, not a strict inequality); this is exactly the perfect-substitutes case
Convexity is undefined for straight-line indifference curves
Straight-line indifference curves always violate monotonicity too
steps.explain: Convexity as defined (mixes are at least as good as the extremes) is satisfied with EQUALITY by straight lines — perfect substitutes are the boundary/degenerate case of convex preferences, not a violation of it. Strict convexity (mixes strictly preferred) is what gives the usual bowed-in shape; ordinary (weak) convexity also allows the flat, straight-line case.

steps.heading: Indifference curves and the utility function
steps.body: Connecting all bundles the consumer is indifferent between traces out an indifference curve. Higher curves (further from the origin, under monotonicity) represent higher satisfaction. A utility function U(x1,x2) is just a way of assigning NUMBERS to bundles so that higher numbers go to more-preferred bundles: X≻Y iff U(X)>U(Y). Crucially, we only care about the ORDER these numbers put bundles in — this is called ordinal utility, as opposed to cardinal utility (where the actual size of the number, or differences between numbers, would carry meaning). Nothing in this course asks 'how much MORE do you like X than Y', only 'do you like X more than Y'.

steps.heading: Monotonic transformations
steps.body: Because only the ORDERING matters, any monotonic (order-preserving) transformation of a utility function represents exactly the same preferences. If U(x1,x2) works, so do log(U), U+k (any constant k), U^n (for U>0), or √U — the ranking of every pair of bundles stays identical. This is genuinely useful: Cobb-Douglas utility U=x1^αx2^(1-α) is algebraically painful to differentiate directly, so economists often take logs first (log U = α·log(x1)+(1-α)·log(x2)) since that's a monotonic transformation and gives IDENTICAL demand — just easier calculus.

steps.q: U(x1,x2)=x1x2 and V(x1,x2)=ln(x1)+ln(x2) (=ln(x1x2), a monotonic transform of U). At bundle A=(4,9), U=36 and V=ln(36)≈3.58. At bundle B=(6,6), U=36 and V=ln(36)≈3.58 also. What can you conclude?
options: A and B must be on different indifference curves since the utility levels don't match a 'nice' number
A and B are on the SAME indifference curve for both U and V, since both give identical utility values at both bundles — consistent with V being a monotonic transform of U
V is not actually a valid transformation of U here
This only holds for these specific numbers and isn't generally true for monotonic transforms
steps.explain: A and B give equal utility under BOTH U and V (36 for U, ≈3.58 for V, at each bundle) — they're on the same indifference curve regardless of which representation you use. This is exactly what 'monotonic transformation preserves preferences' means: the SET of bundles judged equally good doesn't change, even though the numbers attached to them do.

steps.heading: The workhorse case: Cobb-Douglas
steps.body: Between the two extremes of perfect substitutes (straight-line indifference curves, U=aX+bY) and perfect complements (right-angled curves, U=min{aX,bY}), the standard 'nice' case you'll use constantly is Cobb-Douglas: U(x1,x2)=x1^αx2^(1-α), with 0<α<1. It's monotonic (both exponents positive) and strictly convex (diminishing MRS — covered next lesson), giving smooth, well-behaved indifference curves. You'll derive its demand functions explicitly in the Constrained Optimisation lesson, and they turn out to have a beautifully simple form worth memorising.

steps.q: Which of these is the perfect-complements utility function (think: left shoes and right shoes, where extra of one alone is useless without the other)?
options: U(x1,x2)=min{x1,x2}
steps.explain: min{x1,x2} captures 'you're only as well off as your SCARCER good' — having 10 left shoes and 3 right shoes gives you utility 3, since the extra 7 left shoes are useless without matching right shoes. This is the defining feature of perfect complements.

steps.heading: What problem does the MRS solve?
steps.body: We now have two separate pictures: the budget line (what's affordable, with slope -P1/P2 set by the MARKET) and indifference curves (what the consumer wants). To find the optimal choice, we'll eventually need to compare the two slopes. But first we need to properly define the slope of an indifference curve — that's the marginal rate of substitution (MRS), and it represents the consumer's own PERSONAL willingness to trade, as opposed to the market's.

steps.heading: Deriving it from marginal utilities
steps.body:
Suppose the consumer reduces x1 by a small amount Δx1. How much x2 (ΔX2) do they need back to stay on the same indifference curve (same utility)? Using marginal utility MU1=ΔU/Δx1: the utility lost from giving up Δx1 of good 1 is MU1·Δx1. To stay on the same curve, this must be exactly offset by the utility gained from Δx2 more of good 2: MU2·Δx2. Setting them equal: MU1·Δx1 = MU2·Δx2, so Δx2/Δx1 = MU1/MU2. Taking the limit as the changes shrink to zero (using partial derivatives) gives the exact slope:

MRS = dx2/dx1 = (∂U/∂x1)/(∂U/∂x2) = MU1/MU2

(Sign convention note: some textbooks write this with an explicit minus sign since indifference curves slope down; what matters for you is being consistent and recognising MRS = MU1/MU2 as the ratio that gets set equal to the price ratio at the optimum.)

steps.q: U(x1,x2)=x1^2x2. What is MU1 and MU2?
options: MU1=2x1, MU2=x2
MU1=x2, MU2=2x1
steps.explain: MU1=∂U/∂x1=2x1x2 (bring down the power of x1, reduce it by one, x2 untouched). MU2=∂U/∂x2=x1^2 (x2's power is 1, so differentiating just leaves x1^2 behind, since ∂(x2)/∂x2=1).

steps.heading: Worked example: Cobb-Douglas MRS
steps.body:
Take U(x1,x2)=x1^αx2^(1-α). We'll find MU1, MU2, then MRS, spelling out every algebra step so nothing is skipped.

Step 1 — find MU1 = ∂U/∂x1. Treat x2 as a constant and differentiate x1^α using the power rule (bring the exponent down as a multiplier, then reduce the exponent by 1):
∂/∂x1[x1^α] = αx1^(α-1)
The x2^(1-α) factor doesn't involve x1, so it just tags along unchanged:
MU1 = αx1^(α-1)·x2^(1-α)

Step 2 — find MU2 = ∂U/∂x2 the same way, but now treating x1 as the constant and differentiating x2^(1-α):
∂/∂x2[x2^(1-α)] = (1-α)x2^(1-α-1) = (1-α)x2^(-α)
The x1^α factor doesn't involve x2, so it tags along unchanged:
MU2 = (1-α)x1^α·x2^(-α)

Step 3 — form the ratio MRS = MU1/MU2, writing it out in full before cancelling anything:
MRS = [αx1^(α-1)x2^(1-α)] / [(1-α)x1^αx2^(-α)]

Step 4 — split this single fraction into three separate, easier fractions: the constants, the x1 powers, and the x2 powers, and simplify each on its own:
• Constants: α/(1-α)
• x1 powers: x1^(α-1)/x1^α = x1^((α-1)-α) = x1^(-1)
• x2 powers: x2^(1-α)/x2^(-α) = x2^((1-α)-(-α)) = x2^(1-α+α) = x2^1 = x2
(Rule used: when dividing powers of the same base, subtract the bottom exponent from the top one.)

Step 5 — multiply the three simplified pieces back together:
MRS = [α/(1-α)] · x1^(-1) · x2 = [α/(1-α)] · (x2/x1)

Final answer:
MRS = [α/(1-α)]·(x2/x1)

Sanity-check the exponent arithmetic: for x1 we got (α-1)-α = -1, so x1^(-1) = 1/x1 — that's exactly why x1 lands on the BOTTOM of the final fraction. For x2 we got (1-α)-(-α) = 1, so x2^1 = x2 stays on top. If those two exponents ever come out differently for you, that's the step to go back and re-check.

Notice: if you apply a monotonic transformation (multiply the whole utility function by a constant t, or take logs), the extra factors cancel out in this ratio and the MRS is completely unchanged — confirming that the MRS is a genuine property of the underlying preferences, not an artefact of which utility function you happened to write down.

steps.q: For U(x1,x2)=x1^0.75x2^0.25, what is the MRS?

steps.heading: Diminishing MRS and convexity
steps.body: For well-behaved (strictly convex) preferences, the MRS (in absolute value) FALLS as you move down and to the right along an indifference curve — this is diminishing MRS. Intuitively: the more of good 1 you already have relative to good 2, the less of good 2 you're willing to give up for one more unit of good 1 (you're already well-stocked with it). This is exactly what makes indifference curves bow in toward the origin rather than being straight lines.

steps.heading: Special cases: homothetic and quasilinear preferences
steps.body:
Two special structures come up repeatedly and are worth knowing by name:

- Homothetic preferences: the MRS depends ONLY on the ratio x2/x1, not on the absolute scale. Formally, if (x1,x2)≻(y1,y2) then (tx1,tx2)≻(ty1,ty2) for any t>0. Cobb-Douglas is always homothetic (check the formula above — it only involves x2/x1). The practical payoff: when income scales up by some factor t, demand for BOTH goods scales up by exactly t too — the consumption ratio never changes with income.

- Quasilinear preferences: U(x1,x2)=v(x1)+x2 — linear in good 2, but possibly non-linear (e.g. concave) in good 1. Here the MRS depends only on x1 (not on x2 at all), so indifference curves are just vertical translates of one another. The practical payoff: past the point where you're consuming both goods, extra income goes ENTIRELY into good 2 — demand for good 1 stops responding to income changes altogether.

steps.q: A consumer's optimal bundle at income £100 is (x1,x2)=(4,20). Their preferences are known to be homothetic. What is their optimal bundle at income £250 (prices unchanged)?
options: (4,20) — unchanged
Cannot say without knowing the specific utility function
steps.explain: Homothetic preferences scale demand exactly with income: 250/100=2.5, so the new bundle is 2.5×(4,20)=(10,50). This is the single most useful practical consequence of homotheticity — you can rescale a known optimum instantly instead of re-solving.

steps.heading: One more curvature question ahead
steps.body: Homothetic and quasilinear preferences describe how demand responds to income and which axis the MRS depends on. There's a third, related question worth its own lesson: precisely HOW curved is a given indifference curve — how easily does the consumer substitute one good for the other? That's the elasticity of substitution, covered next.

steps.heading: The question this answers
steps.body: You now know the MRS diminishes along a well-behaved indifference curve, and that curves can be more or less bowed. But 'more curved' is vague — the elasticity of substitution σ makes it precise. It asks: if the MRS changes by 1%, by what percentage does the consumption ratio x2/x1 have to change to keep pace, moving along the SAME indifference curve? A curve where a tiny ratio-change swings the MRS a lot is sharply curved (low σ); a curve where the ratio has to move a long way to shift the MRS much at all is nearly flat (high σ).

steps.heading: The formal definition
steps.body:
σ = |%Δ(x2/x1) / %ΔMRS|

The absolute value is there because MRS and x2/x1 typically move in opposite directions along a convex indifference curve, and economists report σ as a positive number. Three benchmark cases pin down the whole scale:

- Perfect complements (U=min{ax1,bx2}, right-angled curves): σ=0. The ratio x2/x1 is FIXED at the kink no matter what — there's no substitutability at all.
- Cobb-Douglas (U=x1^αx2^(1-α)): σ=1 always, for any α. A 1% change in MRS always produces exactly a 1% change in the ratio.
- Perfect substitutes (U=ax1+bx2, straight-line curves): σ=∞. The MRS is constant everywhere along the line, so it takes an infinite ratio-swing to move it at all — the goods are perfectly interchangeable.

steps.q: Which of the three benchmark utility forms has σ=0, meaning the consumer never substitutes between the two goods at all?
options: U=ax1+bx2 (perfect substitutes)
U=x1^αx2^(1-α) (Cobb-Douglas)
U=min{ax1,bx2} (perfect complements)
All three have σ=0
steps.explain: Perfect complements (Leontief preferences) have σ=0 — the consumption ratio is rigidly fixed at ax1=bx2 regardless of relative prices or the MRS, since goods away from that ratio are simply wasted (think left and right shoes).

steps.heading: Curvature and σ: the visual intuition
steps.body: Picture two indifference curves crossing at the same point with the same MRS there, but one is sharply bowed and the other nearly straight. Move a small distance along each toward a 1%-lower MRS. On the sharply bowed curve, you barely have to move — the ratio x2/x1 changes only a little for that MRS change, so σ is LOW. On the nearly-straight curve, you have to slide a long way along it before the MRS drops by that same 1%, meaning the ratio changes a lot for the same MRS change — so σ is HIGH. Less curvature → higher σ. This is why perfect substitutes (a straight line — zero curvature) sit at σ=∞, and perfect complements (a sharp right-angle — infinite curvature at the kink) sit at σ=0.

steps.q: Two goods have an estimated σ=0.2 between them. Are these goods behaving more like close substitutes or more like near-complements?
options: Close substitutes — high substitutability
Near-complements — the consumer strongly prefers to keep them in a near-fixed ratio
Exactly Cobb-Douglas behaviour
Cannot say without also knowing the price ratio
steps.explain: σ=0.2 is close to the σ=0 (perfect complements) end of the scale, well below Cobb-Douglas's σ=1 — the indifference curves are sharply bowed, and the consumer strongly resists moving away from something close to a fixed consumption ratio, much like the shoes example.

steps.heading: Why this matters beyond consumer theory
steps.body: The elasticity of substitution reappears later in the module in producer theory, applied to how easily a firm substitutes capital for labour in production — the same formula, same intuition, just relabelled. Recognising it as one recurring concept (not two unrelated ones) will save you real time when you get there: the maths and the logic are identical, only the two 'goods' being traded off have changed from x1,x2 to labour and capital.

steps.heading: Putting the two halves together
steps.body: We now have both pieces: the budget line (slope -P1/P2, the market's trade-off rate) and the MRS (the consumer's personal trade-off rate). The consumer's problem is to pick the best affordable bundle: max U(x1,x2) subject to P1x1+P2x2=M. Graphically, this means pushing to the highest indifference curve that still touches the budget line — which happens exactly where the two curves are tangent, i.e. where their slopes are equal.

steps.heading: The tangency condition
steps.body:
At an interior optimum (both goods consumed in positive amounts):

MRS = MU1/MU2 = P1/P2

Why must this hold? Suppose instead MU1/MU2=1 but P1/P2=2/3. The consumer is personally willing to give up 1 unit of good 2 to get 1 more unit of good 1 — but the MARKET only requires them to give up 2/3 of a unit. Since they'd happily give up more than the market demands, they gain by buying more of good 1 (and less of good 2). As x1 rises and x2 falls, diminishing MRS kicks in and MU1/MU2 falls — this continues until it exactly equals 2/3, at which point there's no further gain from trading.

steps.q: At a candidate bundle, MRS=0.5 and P1/P2=2. Which direction should the consumer adjust to increase utility?
options: Buy more of good 1, less of good 2
Buy more of good 2, less of good 1
Already optimal — no adjustment needed
Cannot determine without knowing specific quantities
steps.explain: MRS (0.5) is LESS than the price ratio (2): the consumer is only willing to give up half a unit of good 2 for one more of good 1, but the market demands 2 full units of good 2 for that same trade — a bad deal for them. They should move the other way: buy more good 2, less good 1, until MRS rises to meet the price ratio of 2.

steps.heading: When tangency fails: corners and kinks
steps.body:
The interior tangency condition is a NECESSARY condition when both goods are consumed, but it doesn't always apply:

- Corner solutions: if MRS never equals P1/P2 anywhere along the feasible budget line (e.g. the consumer's tastes are strongly tilted toward one good), the optimum sits at a corner where one good's quantity is zero. This happens with perfect substitutes when the price ratio doesn't exactly match a/b — the consumer spends everything on whichever good gives more 'bang per pound'.
- Kinks: with perfect complements (or a kinked budget line), the MRS is UNDEFINED exactly at the kink — there's no single tangent slope to set equal to the price ratio. Instead you solve directly: use the kink condition (e.g. ax1=bx2 for U=min{ax1,bx2}) together with the budget constraint.

steps.heading: A subtlety: non-convexity
steps.body: The tangency condition is necessary but NOT sufficient for an optimum unless preferences are convex. With non-convex (locally 'wiggly' or partly concave) indifference curves, you can have multiple interior tangencies, only some of which are true maxima — others could be local minima or saddle points along the budget line. Convexity is precisely the assumption that guarantees any tangency you find IS the global best point, so you don't need to separately check every candidate.

steps.q: Why does convexity of preferences matter for solving the consumer's problem via the tangency condition?
options: It doesn't matter — tangency always identifies the optimum regardless of curve shape

Convexity guarantees any interior tangency is a TRUE maximum, so you can trust the tangency condition without checking further; without it, a tangency could be a local minimum or one of several candidates
Convexity is only relevant for corner solutions, not interior ones
Convexity ensures the MRS is always positive
steps.explain: With strictly convex preferences, any point where MRS=price ratio is guaranteed to maximise utility on the budget line. Without convexity, some tangencies could be worse than a nearby corner or another tangency — you'd have to compare utility levels across all candidates rather than trusting the first tangency you find.

steps.heading: Solving in practice: the Lagrangian
steps.body:
The formal, general-purpose way to solve max U(x1,x2) s.t. P1x1+P2x2=M is the Lagrangian:

L = U(x1,x2) + λ(M - P1x1 - P2x2)

First-order conditions: ∂L/∂x1 = MU1 - λP1 = 0, and ∂L/∂x2 = MU2 - λP2 = 0. Dividing the first by the second cancels λ and gives MU1/MU2 = P1/P2 — the tangency condition, now derived formally. λ itself has an economic meaning: it's the marginal utility of income (how much extra utility one more pound of income buys you at the optimum) — useful in later welfare comparisons.

steps.heading: Worked example: Marshallian demand for Cobb-Douglas
steps.body:
For U=x1^αx2^(1-α), the previous step gave the tangency condition: [α/(1-α)]·(x2/x1)=P1/P2. Let's solve this together with the budget constraint, one algebra step at a time.

Step 1 — start from the tangency condition and cross-multiply to clear both fractions at once (multiply both sides by (1-α)·x1·P2):
[α/(1-α)]·(x2/x1) = P1/P2
α·x2·P2 = (1-α)·x1·P1

Step 2 — rearrange so P1x1 is isolated on one side. Divide both sides by (1-α):
P1x1 = [α/(1-α)]·P2x2

This says: at the optimum, the amount of money spent on good 1 (P1x1) is a fixed multiple — α/(1-α) — of the amount spent on good 2 (P2x2). Keep this relationship aside; we substitute it into the budget line next.

Step 3 — write out the budget constraint:
P1x1 + P2x2 = M

Step 4 — substitute the Step 2 result for P1x1 into the budget constraint, so everything is in terms of x2 only:
[α/(1-α)]·P2x2 + P2x2 = M

Step 5 — factor P2x2 out of the left-hand side:
P2x2 · [α/(1-α) + 1] = M

Step 6 — simplify the bracket by rewriting 1 as (1-α)/(1-α) so both terms share the same denominator, then add the numerators:
α/(1-α) + (1-α)/(1-α) = [α + (1-α)]/(1-α) = 1/(1-α)
(the +α and -α cancel in the numerator, leaving just 1 on top)

Step 7 — substitute this simplified bracket back in:
P2x2 · [1/(1-α)] = M

Step 8 — multiply both sides by (1-α), then divide both sides by P2 to isolate x2:
x2* = (1-α)M/P2

Step 9 — find x1* the easy way, by plugging x2* back into the Step 2 relationship P1x1=[α/(1-α)]·P2x2:
P1x1 = [α/(1-α)] · P2 · [(1-α)M/P2]
The P2's cancel top and bottom, and the (1-α)'s cancel top and bottom too, leaving:
P1x1 = αM
x1* = αM/P1

Final answer:
x1* = αM/P1   and   x2* = (1-α)M/P2

The result is strikingly clean: the exponent α is literally the FRACTION of income spent on good 1, and (1-α) is the fraction spent on good 2 — regardless of what the actual prices are. This is worth memorising directly (it's called the Cobb-Douglas expenditure-share result) rather than re-deriving from scratch every time — it will save real time in the exam. But make sure you also understand the derivation above, since exam questions sometimes ask you to derive it rather than just quote it.

steps.heading: Comparative statics: how demand responds to changes
steps.body:
Once you have demand functions x*(P1,P2,M), comparative statics asks how the optimum MOVES as one exogenous variable changes, holding the others fixed:

- Income-consumption curve → Engel curve: trace how demand for a good changes as income M rises (prices fixed). Upward-sloping Engel curve = normal good; downward-sloping = inferior good.
- Price-consumption curve → demand curve: trace how demand for a good changes as its OWN price falls (income, other prices fixed). This is the ordinary downward-sloping demand curve you already know, but now it's properly derived from the underlying optimisation rather than just asserted.

Both curves come from the SAME sequence of tangency points — just re-plotted against a different variable on the axis (income, or that good's own price, instead of the other good's quantity).

steps.heading: Marshallian demand elasticities
steps.body:
Three elasticities, all built the same way — a % response divided by a % cause:

Price elasticity: εx,px = (∂x/∂px)(px/x)
Income elasticity: ξx,M = (∂x/∂M)(M/x) — positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods
Cross-price elasticity: ex,py = (∂x/∂py)(py/x) — positive for substitutes, negative for complements

These aren't just abstract formulas — real-world estimates (e.g. cigarettes ≈ -0.94, fresh fruit in the UK ≈ -0.29) show most everyday goods are demand-inelastic (|ε|<1), while specific product variants (individual iPad models, specific wine brands against close substitutes) can be highly elastic.

steps.q: A good has income elasticity ξ=-0.3. What kind of good is this, and what happens to demand if income rises by 10%?
options: Normal good; demand rises by about 3%
Inferior good; demand falls by about 3%
Giffen good; demand falls by about 30%
Luxury good; demand rises by about 30%
steps.explain: Negative income elasticity defines an inferior good. %ΔQ ≈ ξ × %ΔM = -0.3 × 10% = -3%, so demand falls by about 3% when income rises by 10%.

lessons.title: Income and Substitution Effects: Hicks & Slutsky

steps.heading: Why split a price change into two pieces?
steps.body: When the price of a good falls, two things happen simultaneously: (1) the good becomes relatively cheaper compared to the other good, which pulls demand toward it — the substitution effect; and (2) the consumer's real purchasing power rises (their money now buys more), which changes demand depending on whether the good is normal or inferior — the income effect. Untangling how much of the total demand change is 'pure substitution' versus 'feeling richer' is one of the most important techniques in this course, because it's exactly what's needed later for welfare analysis (deadweight loss, tax incidence).

steps.heading: The Hicksian approach: hold utility fixed
steps.body: The cleanest way to isolate the substitution effect is the Hicksian (compensated) method: after the price change, imagine adjusting the consumer's income just enough that they can reach EXACTLY their original utility level again (no better, no worse) — this is like pivoting the budget line to the new price ratio, then sliding it in or out until it's tangent to the ORIGINAL indifference curve. The resulting demand is called Hicksian or compensated demand, written H(P1,P2,v̄) — notice it depends on prices and a target utility level v̄, NOT on income M. This is the crucial contrast with Marshallian demand x*(P1,P2,M), which depends on income.

steps.q: What is the key difference between how Marshallian and Hicksian demand are defined?
options: Marshallian demand depends on (P1,P2,M); Hicksian demand depends on (P1,P2,v̄) for a target utility v̄
They are defined identically, just with different names
Marshallian demand comes from expenditure minimisation; Hicksian from utility maximisation
Hicksian demand only exists for Cobb-Douglas utility functions
steps.explain: Marshallian demand solves 'maximise utility given a fixed budget M' (so it depends on M). Hicksian demand solves 'minimise expenditure given a fixed target utility v̄' (so it depends on v̄ instead) — this is the dual problem, covered in its own lesson.

steps.heading: Worked example, step 1: the initial optimum
steps.body: Take U(x1,x2)=x1^0.5x2^0.5, P1=20, P2=10, M=200. Using the Cobb-Douglas formula from the previous lesson: x1*=0.5(200)/20=5, x2*=0.5(200)/10=10. Utility at this bundle: u=5^0.5×10^0.5=√50≈7.071. Now suppose P1 falls from 20 to 10 — we want to know how much of the resulting change in x1 is substitution, and how much is income.

steps.heading: Worked example, step 2: isolate the substitution effect
steps.body: Minimise expenditure at the NEW prices (P1=10, P2=10) subject to reaching the ORIGINAL utility level (u=7.071). Set up the Lagrangian L=10x1+10x2+λ(7.071-x1^0.5x2^0.5). The FOCs, when divided, give the same tangency structure as before: x2/x1 = P1/P2 = 10/10 = 1, so x1=x2 at this compensated optimum. Substituting into the utility constraint: x1^0.5·x1^0.5=x1=7.071. So the Hicksian (substitution-effect-only) demand is x1=x2=7.071. Good 1 has risen from 5 to 7.071 — a rise of 2.071 — purely because it's now relatively cheaper, with the consumer kept exactly as happy as before (not richer, not poorer).

steps.q: In the worked example, why does the compensated (Hicksian) optimum end up at x1=x2=7.071 rather than staying at the original x1=5, x2=10?
options: Because income was held fixed at £200 throughout
Because even though UTILITY is held fixed, the PRICE RATIO has changed to 1:1, so the tangency condition now requires equal quantities, unlike the original 2:1 price ratio
This is an arithmetic error — it should remain at (5,10)
Because Hicksian demand ignores prices entirely
steps.explain: Utility is held fixed (that's the whole point of the compensation), but the RELATIVE PRICE has changed from P1/P2=20/10=2 to P1/P2=10/10=1. The tangency condition MRS=price ratio now requires a different quantity ratio (x2/x1=1, i.e. equal quantities) to reach the same utility level as cheaply as possible at the new prices — this is the pure substitution response.

steps.heading: Worked example, step 3: isolate the income effect
steps.body: The Hicksian bundle (7.071, 7.071) isn't the consumer's FINAL choice — it's an artificial 'compensated' stopping point that ignores the fact that, at the new prices, the consumer's original £200 now buys MORE utility than before (real income has genuinely risen). To find where they actually end up, go back to ordinary utility maximisation at the new prices with the ORIGINAL income: x1*=0.5(200)/10=10, x2*=0.5(200)/10=10. So the final Marshallian demand is x1=x2=10. The income effect is the gap between this final answer and the Hicksian stopping point: 10 - 7.071 = 2.929 — this is how much further x1 rises purely because the consumer now feels richer.

steps.heading: Putting it together: the full decomposition
steps.body:
Total effect on x1 (5 → 10, a rise of 5) splits into:
Substitution effect: 7.071 - 5 = 2.071 (positive — always positive for a price fall, whatever the good)
Income effect: 10 - 7.071 = 2.929 (positive here, because good 1 is normal — rising real income raises demand for it further)

Check: 2.071 + 2.929 = 5.000 ✓ — the two pieces must always sum exactly to the total effect.

steps.q: For a NORMAL good, do the substitution and income effects of a price FALL point in the same direction or opposite directions?
options: Same direction — both push demand up, reinforcing each other
Opposite directions — substitution pushes demand up, income pushes it down
Same direction, but only for Cobb-Douglas utility specifically
Opposite directions, with income effect always dominating
steps.explain: For a normal good, both effects reinforce: the substitution effect always pushes demand for a now-cheaper good UP, and for a normal good, rising real income ALSO pushes demand up. This is why demand curves for normal goods slope down so unambiguously.

steps.heading: Inferior and Giffen goods: when the effects fight
steps.body:
For an INFERIOR good, the income effect flips sign: rising real income now REDUCES demand (the substitution effect still pushes demand up, since that direction never depends on whether the good is normal or inferior). Two sub-cases:

- Ordinary inferior good: the (still-positive) substitution effect is LARGER in magnitude than the (now-negative) income effect, so total demand still rises when price falls — the good still obeys the law of demand, just less strongly than a normal good would.
- Giffen good: the negative income effect is so large it OUTWEIGHS the positive substitution effect — total demand actually FALLS when price falls, an apparent violation of the law of demand. This requires the good to be both very strongly inferior AND take up a large share of the budget (the classic textbook story is a subsistence staple like bread or potatoes for a very poor household).

steps.q: A good's price falls. The substitution effect on quantity is +8 units. The total effect turns out to be -3 units. What can you conclude about the income effect, and is this a Giffen good?
options: Income effect = -11 units; not enough information to call it Giffen without checking it's also inferior (though a negative income effect exceeding the substitution effect is exactly the Giffen signature)
Income effect = +11 units; this is a normal good
Income effect = -5 units; this cannot be a Giffen good
The numbers are inconsistent and cannot both be true simultaneously
steps.explain: Substitution effect + income effect = total effect, so income effect = total - substitution = -3 - 8 = -11. A negative income effect large enough to flip the TOTAL effect negative (despite a positive substitution effect) is exactly the definition of Giffen behaviour — the good is so strongly inferior that getting richer from the price fall makes the consumer buy noticeably LESS of it, more than offsetting the substitution effect.

steps.heading: A different starting point: from choices to preferences
steps.body: So far we've assumed preferences exist and DERIVED choices from them. Revealed preference theory runs the logic backward: given only OBSERVED choices at various prices, can we recover consistent information about preferences — without ever assuming a specific utility function? This matters because in the real world we usually only see what people bought, not their private mental ranking of every possible bundle.

steps.heading: Directly revealed preferred
steps.body: Suppose at prices (P1,P2) the consumer buys bundle X=(X1,X2), spending their entire budget: P1X1+P2X2=M. Suppose bundle Y=(Y1,Y2) was ALSO affordable at those same prices: P1Y1+P2Y2 ≤ M. Since the consumer could have bought Y but chose X instead, and we assume they're optimising, X must be at least as good as Y in their eyes. We say X is directly revealed preferred to Y, written X≻Y (or ≽, depending on strictness), and formally: P1X1+P2X2 ≥ P1Y1+P2Y2.

steps.q: At prices (3,5), a consumer buys A=(10,4) costing 3(10)+5(4)=50. Bundle B=(5,7) costs 3(5)+5(7)=50 also. Was B directly revealed preferred, or A?
options: A is directly revealed preferred to B, since both cost exactly the same and A was chosen
B is directly revealed preferred to A
Neither — equal cost means no preference is revealed
Not enough information to determine
steps.explain: B was affordable (cost of B = M = cost of A, so B satisfies P1Y1+P2Y2 ≤ M), and A was chosen instead — so A is directly revealed preferred to B. The consumer could have bought exactly B for exactly the same money but chose A.

steps.heading: WARP: the Weak Axiom
steps.body: The Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP) says: if X is directly revealed preferred to Y (at some prices), then Y can NEVER be directly revealed preferred to X (at any other prices) — the preference can't reverse. Formally: if P1X1+P2X2 ≥ P1Y1+P2Y2 (X chosen when Y affordable), then it must NOT be the case that, at different prices (Q1,Q2), Y is chosen while X was affordable there, i.e. NOT(Q1Y1+Q2Y2 ≥ Q1X1+Q2X2). WARP is the minimum consistency check: it looks at each PAIR of observations in isolation.

steps.heading: SARP: closing the loophole
steps.body: WARP only catches DIRECT two-way reversals. But consistency could still fail through an INDIRECT chain: suppose X is revealed preferred to Y, and Y is revealed preferred to Z (two separate pairwise comparisons, both satisfying WARP individually) — but then Z turns out to be directly revealed preferred to X. No single pair here violates WARP, yet the chain X≻Y≻Z≻X is still a genuine preference cycle. The Strong Axiom of Revealed Preference (SARP) closes this gap: it requires consistency across chains of ANY length, not just single pairs — effectively demanding that the revealed preference relation be transitive, the same property we assumed directly for 'proper' preferences back in the Preferences lesson.

steps.q: A dataset satisfies WARP for every single pair of observations checked. Does it automatically satisfy SARP too?
options: Yes — WARP for all pairs is mathematically equivalent to SARP
Not necessarily — WARP only rules out direct two-way reversals; an indirect cycle through three or more observations could still violate SARP while every individual pair satisfies WARP
No — SARP is strictly weaker than WARP, so passing WARP says nothing about SARP
Only true if there are fewer than 3 observations in the dataset
steps.explain: WARP and SARP are genuinely different conditions. WARP checks each pair in isolation; SARP additionally rules out indirect cycles that span three or more observations. A dataset can pass every pairwise WARP check yet still contain a hidden indirect cycle that SARP would catch — that's precisely why SARP is the stronger condition, used when testing consistency across a full dataset of choices rather than just one comparison.

steps.heading: Why this matters beyond the exam
steps.body: Revealed preference is genuinely used in empirical work: if you observe someone's actual purchases across many different price/income situations, WARP and SARP let you TEST whether their behaviour is consistent with any well-behaved underlying preference ordering at all — without ever having to guess or estimate the specific utility function. If real data violates SARP, that's direct evidence against the standard rational-consumer model for that person or group (an important entry point into behavioural economics, which you've already touched on in the Preferences lesson).

steps.q: Bundle A costs £40 at prices where A was bought, and bundle B would have cost £45 at those same prices. What can you conclude about revealed preference between A and B from this alone?
options: A is directly revealed preferred to B
B is directly revealed preferred to A
Nothing directly — B was NOT affordable (£45 > the £40 actually spent), so the affordability condition for direct revealed preference isn't met
A and B must be on the same indifference curve
steps.explain: Direct revealed preference requires the OTHER bundle to have been AFFORDABLE when the chosen one was bought. Here B costs more than was spent (£45 > £40), so B wasn't affordable — the consumer wasn't actually choosing A over an affordable B, so this observation alone reveals nothing about A vs B.

lessons.title: The Dual Problem: Utility Max vs Expenditure Min

steps.heading: Two ways to ask the same question
steps.body: So far we've solved max U(x1,x2) subject to P1x1+P2x2=M — the primal problem: given a fixed budget, get the most utility possible. There's a mirror-image version, the dual problem: min P1x1+P2x2 subject to U(x1,x2)=v̄ — given a fixed TARGET utility level v̄, spend the least money possible to reach it. These aren't just similar in spirit — at the optimum, they describe literally the SAME bundle, just approached from opposite directions.

steps.heading: Why the dual problem exists at all
steps.body: You already met this in the Income & Substitution Effects lesson without naming it: to isolate the substitution effect of a price change, we minimised expenditure subject to reaching the ORIGINAL utility level at the NEW prices. That was the dual problem in action. Its main use throughout the course is exactly this — it's the tool for holding utility (welfare) fixed while prices move, which the primal problem can't do directly since the primal always holds a fixed MONEY budget instead.

steps.q: In the dual problem min P1x1+P2x2 s.t. U(x1,x2)=v̄, what plays the role that income M played in the primal problem?
options: λ, the Lagrange multiplier
The target utility level v̄ — fixed and given, just as M was fixed and given in the primal
There is no equivalent quantity
P1 and P2 together replace the role of M
steps.explain: The roles swap cleanly: in the primal, income M is fixed and utility is maximised; in the dual, utility v̄ is fixed and expenditure is minimised. v̄ is the dual's counterpart to M.

steps.heading: Three ways to solve the SAME optimisation
steps.body:
Whichever problem you're solving (primal or dual), there are three equivalent solution methods, useful to know because sometimes one is much faster than another for a given problem:

1. Equi-marginal principle: directly set MU1/MU2=P1/P2 (the tangency condition) and combine with the constraint.
2. Lagrangian: set up L, take first-order conditions, divide them to eliminate λ and recover the same tangency condition, then combine with the constraint.
3. Unconstrained substitution: solve the constraint for one variable (e.g. x2 in terms of x1), substitute into the objective, and maximise/minimise the resulting single-variable function directly.

All three MUST give identical answers — trying two of them on the same problem is a genuinely good way to catch algebra mistakes under exam pressure.

steps.heading: Worked example: all three methods agree
steps.body:
Maximise U(x1,x2)=x1^0.5x2^0.5 subject to P1=20, P2=10, M=200.

Equi-marginal: MU1/MU2 = x2/x1 = P1/P2 = 2, so x2=2x1. Sub into budget: 20x1+10(2x1)=200 → 40x1=200 → x1=5, x2=10.

Lagrangian: L=x1^0.5x2^0.5+λ(200-20x1-10x2). FOCs: 0.5x1^(-0.5)x2^0.5=20λ, 0.5x1^0.5x2^(-0.5)=10λ. Dividing gives x2/x1=2 — identical tangency condition, same answer: x1=5, x2=10.

Unconstrained: x2=(200-20x1)/10=20-2x1. Substitute: U=x1^0.5(20-2x1)^0.5. Differentiate and set to zero — after simplifying, this also collapses to x1=5, x2=10.

All three: x1*=5, x2*=10. This matches the direct Cobb-Douglas share formula too: x1*=0.5(200)/20=5 ✓.

steps.q: Using the direct Cobb-Douglas formula, verify: for U=x1^0.5x2^0.5, P1=20, P2=10, M=200, what is x2*?
steps.explain: x2*=(1-α)M/P2=0.5(200)/10=100/10=10 — matches all three methods above.

steps.heading: Hicksian demand as the dual's solution
steps.body: When you solve the DUAL problem, the resulting demand functions are exactly the Hicksian (compensated) demands from the previous lesson: H1(P1,P2,v̄) and H2(P1,P2,v̄). They depend on prices and the target utility v̄, not on income — because income was never part of the dual problem's constraint in the first place. This is the formal reason Hicksian demand is sometimes just called 'the solution to the expenditure-minimisation problem'.

steps.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Primal problem → Marshallian demand; Dual problem → Hicksian demand
Primal problem → Hicksian demand; Dual problem → Marshallian demand
Both problems produce Marshallian demand
Both problems produce Hicksian demand
steps.explain: Utility maximisation subject to a budget (the primal) produces Marshallian (uncompensated) demand, a function of prices and income. Expenditure minimisation subject to a utility target (the dual) produces Hicksian (compensated) demand, a function of prices and utility.

steps.heading: Treating time like a good
steps.body: Everything so far in consumer theory involved choosing between two DIFFERENT goods at a single point in time. But the exact same tools apply to a completely different kind of choice: how much to consume NOW versus how much to consume LATER. Should you spend your student loan today or save some of it? How much debt should you take on? How much should you save for retirement? All of these are intertemporal choice problems, and Harkins' approach is refreshingly direct: we treat two time periods (t=1, t=2) EXACTLY like two goods, and re-use every tool from the rest of consumer theory — budget constraints, tangency conditions, Marshallian demand — completely unchanged.

steps.heading: Building the intertemporal budget constraint
steps.body:
Suppose you earn income m1 in period 1 and m2 in period 2, and can freely borrow or lend at interest rate r. If you consume c1 in period 1, you have (m1-c1) left over. If this is positive, you SAVE it, and it earns interest, becoming (1+r)(m1-c1) available in period 2 on top of your period-2 income m2. So the maximum you could consume in period 2 is:

c2 = m2 + (1+r)(m1-c1)

Rearranging this single equation into the familiar 'total value = total value' budget-line form gives two equivalent ways to write it:

Future value form: (1+r)c1 + c2 = (1+r)m1 + m2
(everything measured in period-2 pounds — money not spent in period 1 grows by the factor (1+r))

Present value form: c1 + c2/(1+r) = m1 + m2/(1+r)
(everything measured in period-1 pounds — money to be received in period 2 is 'discounted' back to today by dividing by (1+r))

Both describe the exact same line. In the (c1,c2) diagram, this budget line has slope -(1+r) — exactly playing the role that -(P1/P2) played for ordinary goods. Here, (1+r) is the market's exchange rate between present and future consumption: giving up £1 of consumption today buys you exactly £(1+r) of consumption next period.

steps.q: You earn m1=£10,000 this period and expect m2=£0 next period. The interest rate is r=10%. If you consume c1=0 this period (save everything), what is the maximum you can consume next period?
steps.explain: Using the future-value budget constraint (1+r)c1+c2=(1+r)m1+m2 with c1=0: c2=(1+r)m1+m2=1.1(10,000)+0=£11,000 — your £10,000 grows by the 10% interest rate over the year.

steps.heading: Borrowers and lenders
steps.body:
The point (m1,m2) — your income in each period, with no borrowing or saving at all — is called your ENDOWMENT point, and just like in the ordinary endowment model, the budget line ALWAYS passes through it (choosing to consume exactly your own income each period, trading nothing, is always feasible). Where you actually choose to consume relative to this point defines your role in the credit market:

A LENDER chooses c1 < m1: they consume less than their period-1 income, SAVING (effectively lending out) the difference at rate r, which buys them extra consumption in period 2 beyond m2.

A BORROWER chooses c1 > m1: they consume more than their period-1 income by borrowing against their period-2 income, and must repay that loan with interest, reducing what's left to consume in period 2 below m2.

Graphically, lenders sit on the segment of the budget line to the LEFT of the endowment point (c1<m1), and borrowers sit to the RIGHT of it (c1>m1).

steps.q: A consumer has m1=£40,000 and chooses c1=£55,000. Are they a borrower or a lender?
options: A lender, since they are consuming a large amount
A borrower, since c1 > m1 — they are consuming more than their period-1 income by borrowing against period 2
Cannot be determined without knowing r
Neither — this is only possible if m2 is also given
steps.explain: c1=£55,000 exceeds their period-1 income m1=£40,000, so they must be borrowing £15,000 against their future (period-2) income to fund this consumption — making them a borrower, regardless of the specific interest rate or m2.

steps.heading: Worked example: solving the two-period optimisation problem
steps.body:
Take a consumer with m1=£100, m2=£55, facing interest rate r=10%, and Cobb-Douglas preferences over consumption timing: U(c1,c2)=c1^0.5c2^0.5.

Step 1 — convert the problem into a form you already know how to solve. Using the present-value budget constraint c1 + c2/(1+r) = m1 + m2/(1+r), treat the RIGHT-HAND SIDE as a single number — 'present-value wealth':
PV wealth = m1 + m2/(1+r) = 100 + 55/1.1 = 100 + 50 = £150

Step 2 — notice the present-value budget constraint c1 + c2/(1+r) = 150 has EXACTLY the same shape as an ordinary budget constraint P1x1+P2x2=M, with 'price' P1=1 (for c1) and 'price' P2=1/(1+r) (for c2, since future consumption is discounted). So you can apply the Cobb-Douglas demand formula directly:
c1* = α × (PV wealth)/P1 = 0.5 × 150/1 = £75
c2* = (1-α) × (PV wealth)/P2 = 0.5 × 150/(1/1.1) = 0.5 × 150 × 1.1 = £82.5

Step 3 — check against the budget constraint and classify borrower/lender. Since c1*=£75 is LESS than m1=£100, this consumer SAVES £25 today — they are a LENDER. Check c2: c2 should equal m2+(1+r)(m1-c1*) = 55 + 1.1(100-75) = 55 + 1.1(25) = 55+27.5 = £82.5 ✓ — matches exactly.

steps.q: Continuing the worked example (m1=100, m2=55, r=10%, U=c1^0.5c2^0.5), what is the present-value wealth, and is the consumer a borrower or lender?
options: PV wealth=£155; borrower
PV wealth=£150; lender, since c1*=£75 < m1=£100
PV wealth=£150; borrower, since c2* > c1*
PV wealth=£145; lender
steps.explain: PV wealth = m1+m2/(1+r) = 100+55/1.1 = 100+50 = £150. Solving gives c1*=£75 < m1=£100, so the consumer consumes less than their period-1 income and saves the rest — making them a lender.

steps.heading: Opportunity cost and extending to many periods
steps.body:
The two-period model generalises cleanly. The OPPORTUNITY COST of consuming £1 today, in an N-period model with a constant interest rate r, is £(1+r)^(N-1) at time N — because £10,000 invested today becomes £10,000(1+r) after one year, £10,000(1+r)^2 after two years, and £10,000(1+r)^n after n years (compound interest).

With n different income amounts m1, m2, ..., mn across n periods (all earning/costing interest at the same constant rate r), the present value of the WHOLE income stream generalises the two-period formula:

PV = m1 + m2/(1+r) + m3/(1+r)^2 + ... + mn/(1+r)^(n-1)

Each future income payment is discounted back to period-1 pounds by dividing by (1+r) raised to however many periods away it is. This is exactly the same idea used to value pensions, mortgages, bonds, and any other stream of payments spread across time.

steps.q: An income stream pays m1=£1,000, m2=£1,100, m3=£1,210, with a constant interest rate r=10%. What is the present value?
options: £3,310 (just summed with no discounting)
£3,000, since each payment discounts back to exactly £1,000 in present-value terms
steps.explain: PV = m1 + m2/(1+r) + m3/(1+r)^2 = 1,000 + 1,100/1.1 + 1,210/1.21 = 1,000+1,000+1,000 = £3,000. (This income stream was deliberately constructed to grow at exactly rate r each period, so every term discounts back to the same £1,000 — a useful pattern to recognise quickly.)

steps.heading: Comparative statics: what happens when the interest rate changes?
steps.body:
Because the budget line always pivots around the FIXED endowment point (m1,m2) — never shifting away from it, only rotating around it — revealed preference gives us clean, general answers about who gains and who loses when r changes, WITHOUT needing to know anyone's specific utility function:

If r RISES: the budget line becomes STEEPER (slope -(1+r) becomes more negative), pivoting around (m1,m2). A LENDER's original choice remains exactly affordable, and strictly more is now available on the lending side (money saved earns more interest) — so a lender is unambiguously BETTER OFF and remains a lender. A BORROWER faces a shrinking feasible region on their side — their original choice may become unaffordable, so they may remain a borrower (just borrowing less) or the higher cost of debt may push them to switch entirely to becoming a lender instead — genuinely ambiguous without more information.

If r FALLS: exactly the mirror image. A BORROWER is unambiguously better off (borrowing is now cheaper) and remains a borrower. A LENDER may remain a lender or may switch to becoming a borrower instead — ambiguous.

steps.q: The interest rate r falls. A consumer who was previously a LENDER — what can we say about their wellbeing and whether they remain a lender?
options: They are unambiguously better off and remain a lender
Ambiguous — they may remain a lender or might switch to becoming a borrower, since a fall in r shrinks the feasible region on the lending side
They are unambiguously worse off but always remain a lender
Nothing changes for a lender when r falls
steps.explain: A fall in r makes the budget line flatter, pivoting around the endowment point (m1,m2) — this shrinks the feasible region on the LENDING side (saving now earns less interest) while expanding it on the borrowing side. A lender's original bundle may no longer be optimal or even preferred, so it is genuinely ambiguous whether they remain a lender or switch to borrowing — this is the mirror image of the 'r rises' case for borrowers covered just before.

steps.heading: Why this matters: real applications
steps.body: This simple two-good relabelling trick — consumption today vs. consumption tomorrow, connected by the interest rate acting as a relative price — underpins a huge range of real economic questions: how much student debt is worth taking on, how retirement savings respond to interest rate changes, how a rise in the Bank of England base rate affects borrowers versus savers very differently (exactly the ambiguous/unambiguous comparative statics above), and how governments think about the effects of policies that change borrowing costs. It's also exactly the same mathematical structure used later in EC202 for modelling saving, investment and asset markets — mastering it here pays off well beyond this one topic.

lessons.title: Endowments and the Revised Slutsky Equation

steps.heading: What is an endowment?
steps.body:
Every consumer theory problem so far assumed a consumer starts with a fixed pot of MONEY (income M) and buys goods with it. But in many real situations, people instead start with a bundle of GOODS they already own — an endowment (w1,w2) — which they can sell (in part or in full) and use the proceeds to buy other things instead. Think of a farmer who grows wheat and wants to eat some bread and sell the rest, or a worker whose only 'endowment' is hours in the day.

Formally, an endowment is a bundle of goods (w1,w2) owned by the consumer and tradable for other goods at market prices. Given prices p1, p2, the consumer's budget constraint becomes:

p1x1 + p2x2 = p1w1 + p2w2

The right-hand side — the total market VALUE of the endowment — plays exactly the role that fixed income M used to play. But crucially, this 'income' is now ENDOGENOUS: it depends on the prices p1 and p2, which is a genuinely new feature compared to everything covered so far.

steps.heading: The budget line always passes through the endowment point
steps.body:
Here is the single most important structural fact about endowment budget constraints: whatever the prices are, the budget line ALWAYS passes through the point (w1,w2) itself. Why? Because choosing x=(w1,w2) exactly — trading nothing at all, just consuming what you already own — is always feasible and uses up exactly the value you started with:

p1w1 + p2w2 = p1w1 + p2w2  (trivially true, for any prices)

So as prices change, the budget line doesn't shift around freely the way an exogenous-income budget line does — it PIVOTS around the fixed point (w1,w2).

Worked example: you own an endowment of (w1,w2)=(5,10) — say, 5 jumpers and 10 pairs of jeans — with prices p1=£40 (jumpers) and p2=£20 (jeans). Your budget constraint is 40x1+20x2=40(5)+20(10)=200+200=£400. Now suppose jeans go on sale at 50% off, so p2 falls to £10. Your new budget constraint is 40x1+10x2=40(5)+10(10)=200+100=£300 — notice this STILL passes through (5,10): 40(5)+10(10)=300 ✓ — but your total wealth has FALLEN from £400 to £300, purely because the goods you own became less valuable, even though you didn't sell anything.

steps.q: Whatever the prices p1 and p2 are, the endowment budget line p1x1+p2x2=p1w1+p2w2 must always pass through which point?
options: The origin (0,0)
The endowment point (w1,w2) itself — since 'trade nothing' is always feasible and always uses up exactly your endowment's value
The point where x1=x2
It depends on the specific prices and cannot be stated in general
steps.explain: Substituting x=(w1,w2) into the budget constraint gives p1w1+p2w2=p1w1+p2w2, an identity that holds for ANY prices — meaning consuming exactly your own endowment is always affordable, so the line must always run through that point, however p1 and p2 move.

steps.heading: Net buyers and net sellers
steps.body:
Given the optimal choice x1* (found the usual way, via tangency of an indifference curve with this budget line), the consumer's relationship to the market for good 1 is classified by comparing x1* to their endowment w1:

Net buyer (net demander): x1* > w1 — the consumer buys MORE of good 1 than they started with, funding this by selling off some of their good-2 endowment.

Net seller (net supplier): x1* < w1 — the consumer sells off part of their good-1 endowment, using the proceeds to buy more of good 2.

This distinction turns out to matter a great deal for how demand responds to price changes, which is where the story gets genuinely new relative to the fixed-income model.

steps.q: A consumer has endowment w1=10 and, after optimising, chooses x1*=6.25. Are they a net buyer or net seller of good 1?
options: Net buyer, since 6.25 is a positive number
Net seller, since x1*=6.25 is LESS than their endowment w1=10 — they sell off the remaining 3.75 units
Neither — this can only be determined from p1 directly
Net buyer, since they are consuming most of their endowment
steps.explain: x1*=6.25 falls short of the endowment w1=10, meaning the consumer holds onto only 6.25 units for themselves and sells the other 3.75 units — the defining feature of a net seller.

steps.heading: Endogenous vs exogenous income: why a price change now has an extra effect
steps.body: With an ordinary fixed money income M, a change in p1 affects demand through exactly two channels you already know: the substitution effect and the ordinary income effect (real purchasing power of a FIXED budget M changes). With an endowment, there's a THIRD channel: changing p1 also changes the MONEY VALUE of what the consumer owns (specifically, p1w1), so their effective income m=p1w1+p2w2 shifts too — even though M was never fixed in the first place. This extra channel is called the endowment income effect.

steps.heading: Deriving the revised Slutsky equation
steps.body:
Putting all three channels together gives the revised Slutsky equation:

∂x1/∂p1 = ∂x1^h/∂p1 + (w1-x1)·(∂x1/∂m)

where ∂x1^h/∂p1 is the (always negative) Hicksian substitution effect, and (w1-x1)·(∂x1/∂m) bundles together BOTH income effects (ordinary + endowment) into a single term.

Compare this to the ordinary Slutsky equation for fixed money income:

∂x1/∂p1 = ∂x1^h/∂p1 - x1·(∂x1/∂m)

Notice the revised equation reduces EXACTLY to the ordinary one when w1=0 (no endowment of good 1 at all — pure money income), since then (w1-x1)=(0-x1)=-x1. This is a useful consistency check: the endowment model doesn't contradict the earlier theory, it strictly generalises it.

The term (w1-x1) has a clean economic meaning: it is exactly the net amount of good 1 the consumer is SELLING (positive if w1>x1, a net seller; negative if w1<x1, a net buyer, since then w1-x1<0).

steps.q: In the revised Slutsky equation, what happens to the term (w1-x1)·(∂x1/∂m) if the consumer is a net BUYER (x1*>w1) of a NORMAL good, when p1 rises?
options: It is positive, opposing the substitution effect
It is negative, since (w1-x1)<0 for a net buyer and ∂x1/∂m>0 for a normal good — this REINFORCES the (always negative) substitution effect, making the total effect unambiguously negative
It is exactly zero for any net buyer
It cannot be signed without further information
steps.explain: For a net buyer, x1*>w1, so (w1-x1)<0. For a normal good, ∂x1/∂m>0. Multiplying a negative by a positive gives a negative endowment-income term — which points the SAME way as the substitution effect (also negative), so a price rise unambiguously reduces demand for a net buyer of a normal good.

steps.heading: Worked example: applying the revised equation to a net seller
steps.body:
Take a consumer with endowment (w1,w2)=(10,5), Cobb-Douglas preferences U(x1,x2)=x1^0.5x2^0.5, facing initial prices p1=2, p2=1.

Step 1 — find initial income and demand: m=p1w1+p2w2=2(10)+1(5)=25. x1*=0.5(25)/2=6.25. Since x1*=6.25 < w1=10, this consumer is a net SELLER of good 1 (selling 3.75 units).

Step 2 — now suppose p1 rises to 3. New income: m'=3(10)+1(5)=35 (income RISES, because the value of the good-1 endowment they're selling went up). New demand: x1*=0.5(35)/3≈5.83.

Step 3 — interpret the total effect: Δx1 = 5.83-6.25 = -0.417, a small DECREASE — even though this consumer is a net seller whose income actually rose when the price went up (which should, other things equal, push a normal good's consumption UP via the income effect), the substitution effect away from the now-pricier good 1 was strong enough to still dominate, producing a net decrease overall. This illustrates exactly why the net-seller case is genuinely AMBIGUOUS in principle — here substitution happened to win, but for different preferences or a bigger endowment, the income effect could instead have won and demand could have risen.

steps.q: In the worked example above (net seller, w1=10, price rises from 2 to 3), why does the consumer's endogenous income RISE even though they end up consuming slightly less of good 1?
options: This is a contradiction — the numbers must be wrong

Because they are a NET SELLER of good 1: a higher p1 raises the market value of the endowment they are selling (p1w1), raising their money income m, even though the substitution effect still pulls their own consumption of good 1 down slightly
Because good 1 is inferior
Income cannot rise when a price rises, by definition
steps.explain: As a net seller, this consumer earns money by SELLING units of good 1 above what they keep — so a higher price for the good they're selling directly raises their income (m=p1w1+p2w2 rises when p1 rises, since w1>0). This is entirely separate from what happens to their own chosen CONSUMPTION x1*, which is instead governed by the (in this case dominant) substitution effect pulling it down.

steps.heading: Why endowments matter beyond textbook goods
steps.body: The endowment framework generalises far beyond literal goods like jumpers and jeans. Labour supply is a classic application: your 'endowment' is a fixed number of hours in the day, the wage is the 'price' of the good you're selling (your labour/time), and a wage change has exactly this same three-way decomposition — substitution, ordinary income, and endowment income effects (this is precisely why labour supply curves can bend backward at high wages: the endowment income effect from a wage rise can outweigh the substitution effect that would otherwise push people to work more). It's also the natural framework for savers and borrowers of capital, for owners of natural resources, and — as you'll see next — for intertemporal choice, where your endowment of income across time periods (m1,m2) plays exactly this same role.

lessons.title: Behavioural Economics: Present Bias and Sin Taxes

steps.heading: Discounting: why £100 tomorrow is worth less than £100 today
steps.body:
Everything in the Intertemporal Choice lesson assumed a consumer compares present and future consumption via a market interest rate r. But even setting markets aside, people psychologically DISCOUNT future payoffs relative to present ones: decisions taken over time involve applying a discount factor δ<1, so that £100 arriving in one year is only worth δ×£100 to you today. Reasons to discount include opportunity cost (money now can be invested), impatience (a genuine preference for consuming sooner), and simple uncertainty (a promised future payoff might never actually arrive).

Under standard EXPONENTIAL discounting, a payoff n years away is worth δ^n today — the SAME discount factor δ applied repeatedly, once per year. A payoff in two years is worth δ²×£100, in three years δ³×£100, and so on.

steps.heading: Worked example: testing for time-consistency
steps.body:
Consider two offers, taken directly from lecture material:

Offer 1: (A) £200 today, or (B) £205 in 1 week.
Offer 2: (A) £200 in 20 weeks, or (B) £205 in 21 weeks.

Under exponential discounting with weekly discount factor δ, preferring option A in Offer 1 means 200 > 205δ. Now check what exponential discounting predicts for Offer 2: comparing 200δ^20 (option A, valued today) against 205δ^21 (option B, valued today). Dividing BOTH sides by the common factor δ^20 gives exactly 200 > 205δ — the SAME inequality as before. In other words, exponential discounting predicts that shifting BOTH payoffs equally far into the future (from 'now vs. 1 week' to '20 weeks vs. 21 weeks') can never flip which option you prefer. This property is called time-consistency.

steps.q: Under standard exponential discounting, if a consumer prefers £200 today over £205 in 1 week, what must they prefer in the choice between £200 in 20 weeks and £205 in 21 weeks?
options: £205 in 21 weeks — the far future is always discounted more heavily so the larger amount wins
£200 in 20 weeks — the SAME relative preference, since exponential discounting is time-consistent and shifting both dates equally doesn't change the comparison
They must be exactly indifferent between the two options
It depends on the specific value of δ and cannot be determined in general
steps.explain: Dividing both delayed values by the common factor δ^20 recovers exactly the original Offer 1 inequality — exponential discounting always predicts the same choice regardless of how far both options are pushed into the future, as long as the GAP between them (here, always exactly 1 week) stays the same.

steps.heading: The behavioural puzzle: many people flip their answer
steps.body:
Empirically, a very common pattern is: people choose (A) £200 TODAY in Offer 1, but then choose (B) £205 in 21 weeks in Offer 2 — a reversal of the underlying 'sooner vs. later, same £5 premium' trade-off. As just shown, this reversal is IMPOSSIBLE to generate from any single, constant exponential discount rate δ. It is the classic empirical signature of present bias: people apply an extra, specific discount to whatever is available RIGHT NOW, over and above their normal patience between any two future dates.

This is modelled with quasi-hyperbolic ('beta-delta') discounting: utility = u(c0) + β[δu(c1) + δ²u(c2) + δ³u(c3) + ...], where β<1 is an EXTRA discount factor applied only to everything beyond right now, layered on top of the ordinary per-period discount δ. Setting β=1 recovers standard, time-consistent exponential discounting exactly as a special case.

steps.q: In the beta-delta model utility = u(c0) + β[δu(c1)+δ²u(c2)+...], what does β<1 specifically capture that δ alone cannot?
options: The overall level of impatience between any two future periods, which δ already fully captures on its own

An EXTRA discount applied specifically to the gap between 'right now' and any future period, on top of the ordinary between-period discount δ — this is what produces the present-bias reversal that a single δ cannot generate
The consumer's risk aversion
The market interest rate
steps.explain: δ alone (with β=1) treats every one-period gap identically, whether it's 'now vs. next period' or 'period 19 vs. period 20' — this is time-consistent and cannot produce a preference reversal. β<1 breaks that symmetry by applying an extra penalty specifically to the future relative to right now, which is exactly the ingredient needed to match the Offer 1/Offer 2 reversal.

steps.heading: Applying present bias: the sin tax model (O'Donoghue and Rabin, 2003)
steps.body:
A well-known application of present bias, studied in the module, models a consumer choosing between a harmful good ('crisps', x — pleasure now, health cost later), a healthy good ('carrots', y), and money (z), each period. Because the consumer is present-biased (β<1), they systematically UNDERWEIGHT the delayed health cost of crisps relative to the immediate pleasure — leading them to consume MORE crisps than even their own fully-patient, long-run self would want.

A benevolent government, wanting to maximise consumers' TRUE welfare (not just their present-biased in-the-moment choices), can respond with a tax on the harmful good. This raises its effective price TODAY, nudging present-day consumption of crisps down toward the level that better reflects the consumer's own genuine long-run interest. This is the core economic logic behind real-world sin taxes on sugary drinks, alcohol, tobacco, and gambling.

steps.q: Why can a sin tax make a present-biased consumer genuinely BETTER OFF, in a way that contradicts the standard 'all taxes reduce welfare' result from ordinary consumer theory?
options: Because sin taxes always raise more government revenue than other taxes

Because standard welfare analysis assumes a consumer's own choices always reflect their true best interest (revealed preference) — but present bias breaks this link, so a tax that corrects the resulting over-consumption can raise true welfare rather than just create deadweight loss
Because the demand for harmful goods is always perfectly inelastic
Sin taxes cannot actually make anyone better off — this is a common misconception
steps.explain: The standard deadweight-loss argument against taxation relies entirely on treating the consumer's freely chosen bundle as the correct benchmark for their welfare. Present bias means the bundle actually chosen (driven by β<1) is systematically distorted away from what the consumer's own fully-patient self would prefer — so a tax that pulls consumption back toward that undistorted level can genuinely help, not just transfer surplus to the government.

steps.heading: Why this challenges the standard rational choice model
steps.body: Every other welfare tool in this course — Marshallian and Hicksian demand, consumer surplus, compensating and equivalent variation — rests on the assumption that a consumer's own choices ARE the correct measure of their own wellbeing (revealed preference). Present bias breaks this link directly: the period-0 self and the period-1 self can genuinely disagree about what's best, so what gets chosen in the moment is no longer automatically the right benchmark for welfare. This is precisely why the syllabus frames behavioural economics as a 'critique of the rational choice framework' — it isn't that people behave randomly or irrationally in every sense, but that a single, time-consistent utility-maximising agent (the assumption underlying everything else in this course) fails to describe real intertemporal choices, with real, measurable, and policy-relevant consequences.
